records.text: In B. N. Muttoo and another v. T. K. Nandi, Civil Appeal No. 2302 of 1977, the Supreme Court of India considered the landlord's appeal by special leave against the Delhi High Court's order allowing the respondent-tenant's revision, setting aside the Rent Controller's eviction order, and remanding the proceedings. The principal dispute concerned whether Muttoo could invoke the special possession entitlement under section 14A(1) of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958, despite having retired from Government service before receiving the Government's notice to vacate his allotted accommodation and before filing his eviction petition. The Supreme Court allowed the landlord's appeal and held that retirement before service of the Government notice did not, by itself, exclude the landlord from section 14A benefits.
records.stage: Supreme Court appeal and final disposition

records.text: B. N. Muttoo, the appellant-landlord and former Inspector General of Police, leased property No. F-9, East of Kailash, New Delhi, to T. K. Nandi from 15 September 1972 at a monthly rent of Rs. 2,200, excluding electricity and water charges. The lease permitted residential and/or professional purposes but excluded commercial purposes. Following renewals, Nandi became a monthly tenant under the Delhi Rent Control Act. This F-9 property was the tenanted property from which Muttoo sought recovery of possession. It was distinct from the Government-allotted accommodation at C-II/77, Moti Bagh I, New Delhi, which Muttoo occupied while in Government service.
records.stage: Underlying tenancy and property identification

records.text: On 18 July 1974, Muttoo filed an earlier eviction petition against Nandi alleging misuse, subletting, and bona fide requirement. That petition was registered as Suit No. 182 of 1974 and remained pending when the Supreme Court judgment recorded its procedural history. The filing and pendency were recorded facts; the allegations underlying that earlier petition were not independently established or finally adjudicated by the Supreme Court in this appeal.
records.stage: Earlier eviction proceeding

records.text: The Central Government adopted a policy decision on 9 September 1975 requiring Government servants who owned houses in the relevant Delhi area to vacate Government accommodation allotted to them within three months beginning 1 October 1975. The judgment describes this decision as the policy background for the subsequent statutory amendment. The policy concerned Government servants, whereas the enacted section 14A used the broader expression 'person'.
records.stage: Government policy and legislative background

records.text: Muttoo retired as Inspector General of Police on 30 November 1975. While in office, he had occupied Government-allotted premises at C-II/77, Moti Bagh I, New Delhi. On 9 December 1975, a notice was served on him by the Deputy Director (Administration), referring to the Government's Office Memorandum dated 9 September 1975 and requiring qualifying Government officials who owned houses in Delhi or New Delhi to vacate their allotted Government residences before the stipulated deadline. The notice warned that noncompliance would attract a penal or market-rate licence charge and necessary eviction action. The judgment establishes the notice and its stated consequences, not that Muttoo actually paid such charges or that the Government completed eviction from its accommodation.
records.stage: Retirement and Government accommodation notice

records.text: On 9 December 1975, the same day that the Government notice was served, Muttoo instituted the present eviction proceeding against Nandi under section 14A(1). Nandi applied for leave to defend on 16 January 1976. On 10 March 1976, the Rent Controller refused leave to defend and decreed eviction in favour of the landlord. The Rent Controller treated the landlord's retirement status at the dates of notice and application as irrelevant to eligibility under the statutory requirements, viewed section 14A as a distinct cause of action from the earlier petition, and rejected the argument that mixed residential and professional letting prevented relief under the special provision. These were the Rent Controller's determinations, not independent Supreme Court findings on every aspect of the underlying facts.
records.stage: Section 14A petition and Rent Controller decision

records.text: In seeking leave to contest Muttoo's section 14A eviction petition, Nandi raised three principal objections. First, he argued that Muttoo could not use the special procedure under section 25B because Muttoo was no longer a Government servant when the petition was filed. Second, he asserted that the pending 1974 eviction proceeding prevented the later proceeding because the same ground was already before the Rent Controller. Third, he contended that the F-9 premises had been let for residential and professional purposes rather than exclusively residential use, and therefore the landlord could not obtain eviction on the asserted ground. These propositions were the tenant's objections; the Court did not adopt their claimed legal consequences.
records.stage: Tenant's application for leave to contest

records.text: The Delhi High Court accepted Nandi's revision and set aside the Rent Controller's eviction order, remanding the proceedings to the Rent Controller for disposal according to law. Its principal contrary conclusion was that Muttoo had retired on 30 November 1975, before the amending Ordinance became operative on 1 December 1975, and was consequently liable to vacate Government accommodation independently of his ownership of the disputed tenanted property. On that reasoning, the High Court considered the section 14A eviction application unavailable to him. The remand was ordered by the High Court, not by the Supreme Court. The Supreme Court subsequently rejected the High Court's restrictive statutory interpretation.
records.stage: Delhi High Court revision and remand

records.text: Section 14A(1), as reproduced and interpreted by the Supreme Court, confers a special right on a landlord who is a person occupying residential premises allotted by the Central Government or a local authority and who is required, by or pursuant to a general or special order of that authority, to vacate the allotted accommodation or incur specified obligations in default because the landlord owns residential accommodation in Delhi in the landlord's own name or in the name of a wife or dependent child. When the statutory requirements are satisfied, the right to recover possession of premises let out by that landlord accrues from the qualifying order. The Court identified these requirements as the operative statutory test. This statement describes the adopted test and its conditional legal effect; it does not constitute a separate independent finding that every input to a formal rule calculation has been verified.
records.stage: Supreme Court analysis of section 14A eligibility

records.text: The Supreme Court rejected the proposition that section 14A benefits were confined to persons still serving as Government employees. The enacted provision used the word 'person' rather than 'Government servant', and the Court held that this choice could not be treated as inadvertent or read down to the narrower class covered by the Government's policy. Government-allotted accommodation was not restricted to serving officials, and the legislative purpose was to facilitate recovery of Government accommodation by enabling qualifying allottees to recover premises they had let to tenants. Consequently, Muttoo's retirement before receiving the Government notice did not by itself bar the statutory benefit. The Court expressly declined to agree with the High Court on this issue.
records.stage: Supreme Court statutory interpretation of retirement objection

records.text: The Supreme Court acknowledged that the Government circular of 9 September 1975 and the individual notice served on Muttoo supported a narrower Government-servant-focused policy account. It also recognized why the High Court's interpretation could appear understandable in light of that policy. Nevertheless, the Court treated the enacted language of section 14A as controlling and refused to restrict 'person' to serving Government servants. The Government policy was therefore relevant contrary interpretive material, not a statutory condition independently excluding retired allottees.
records.stage: Supreme Court consideration of Government policy and contrary interpretation

records.text: The Supreme Court addressed Nihal Chand v. Kalyan Chand Jain as a reported precedent that had expressed some sympathy for restricting section 14A benefits in cases involving retired or transferred Government servants. The earlier case did not finally decide the question presented here. As described in the present judgment, its relevant notice had been served before retirement, so entitlement could be explained by the right arising while the landlord was still in service. In Muttoo's case the notice was served after retirement. The Supreme Court accordingly confronted a materially different timing question and resolved it through the enacted meaning of 'person'.
records.stage: Supreme Court treatment of Nihal Chand precedent

records.text: Nandi's mixed-use objection depended on the distinction between premises let for residential purposes alone and premises let for residential as well as professional purposes. The Supreme Court accepted that the F-9 lease included both residential and professional purposes, but distinguished section 14A from section 14(1)(e). The Court explained that section 14A focuses on residential accommodation owned by the landlord and does not repeat section 14(1)(e)'s residential-letting requirement. The F-9 premises had been constructed under the Delhi Development Authority's residential scheme, and their residential character was not lost merely because the lease permitted professional use. The Supreme Court therefore rejected mixed-use letting as a bar to Muttoo's section 14A application.
records.stage: Supreme Court consideration of mixed residential and professional letting

records.text: In distinguishing the two statutory grounds, the Supreme Court discussed earlier decisions concerning premises let for combined residential and professional or commercial purposes. It reported that such authorized mixed use could prevent eviction under the residential-letting ground considered in those authorities. These decisions supplied a comparison with section 14(1)(e) and related earlier legislation; their findings about actual professional activity concerned different tenancies and were not findings that Nandi conducted particular professional activities inside F-9. The Court expressly found it unnecessary to resolve whether predominantly residential letting with permission to use an insignificant part for professional purposes would satisfy the separate residential-letting terminology.
records.stage: Comparison with section 14(1)(e) and reported mixed-use precedents

records.text: Nandi also maintained that Muttoo's pending 1974 eviction petition prevented the later section 14A proceeding. The Rent Controller rejected this position because section 14A provided a new cause of action distinct from the earlier petition. The Supreme Court independently rejected the contention that pendency of the earlier application made the present application impermissible. It reasoned that the section 14A petition rested on different statutory grounds and on special rights conferred in connection with Government-allotted accommodation. The Court did not determine whether the earlier allegations of misuse, subletting, or bona fide requirement were true.
records.stage: Earlier-petition objection and Supreme Court determination

records.text: The Supreme Court addressed the statutory test for leave to defend under section 25B. Under section 25B(4), a tenant wishing to resist an eviction application under section 14A must file an affidavit stating the proposed grounds of contest and obtain leave from the Rent Controller. Under section 25B(5), leave depends on whether the affidavit discloses facts which would disentitle the landlord from obtaining possession under the specified statutory ground. The Court emphasized that this is a restricted inquiry, different from the general Civil Procedure Code approach to leave to defend. For section 14A, it identified potentially relevant disqualifying matters concerning the landlord's occupation of qualifying Government-allotted residential premises and the existence of a qualifying governmental order requiring vacatur on the statutory terms. This was the Court's adopted interpretation of the leave standard, not a finding that Nandi established either of those disqualifying matters.
records.stage: Supreme Court review of leave to contest under sections 25B(4) and 25B(5)

records.text: Applying its construction of section 14A and section 25B, the Supreme Court rejected the legal effect that Nandi sought to attach to Muttoo's retirement, the pending earlier petition, and the mixed residential and professional letting. Retirement before the notice was not an additional statutory disqualification; the earlier petition involved different grounds; and section 14A did not require exclusive residential letting. The existence of these objections and the facts supporting their formulation must be distinguished from their capacity to defeat the statutory entitlement. The judgment reports the principal objections raised in Nandi's leave application but does not reproduce the entire supporting affidavit.
records.stage: Supreme Court application of section 25B to the principal objections

records.text: Counsel for Nandi advanced a further statutory argument that a landlord proceeding under section 14A should also satisfy the requirements of section 14(1)(e), relying on the relationship between sections 25B, 25C, 14(6), and 14(7). This was an argument by the tenant's counsel, not the Supreme Court's adopted construction. The Supreme Court considered it after addressing the earlier objections and rejected the proposed additional requirements, explaining the distinct functions of the section 25C modifications.
records.stage: Supreme Court consideration of sections 25B, 25C and proposed additional section 14(1)(e) requirements

records.text: The Supreme Court explained that section 14(6) ordinarily imposes a five-year restriction where a landlord acquired premises by transfer and seeks recovery under section 14(1)(e). Section 25C(1), however, makes that restriction inapplicable to a landlord satisfying the requirements of section 14A. The Court treated this as a statutory exception to the transfer-related restriction rather than as a reason to incorporate all section 14(1)(e) conditions into section 14A. It did not make a case-specific finding establishing a particular date on which Muttoo acquired F-9 by transfer.
records.stage: Supreme Court interpretation of the five-year transfer restriction

records.text: The Supreme Court further held that the special right described as immediate recovery under section 14A remains subject to section 25C(2). That subsection substitutes two months for the six-month period otherwise prescribed by section 14(7) in the relevant cases, including eviction orders under section 14A. Accordingly, a qualifying landlord is not entitled to obtain possession before two months have elapsed from the applicable order for recovery of possession. This ruling establishes a legal waiting-period requirement, not that possession of F-9 was actually delivered to Muttoo on any particular date.
records.stage: Supreme Court interpretation of post-order possession timing

records.text: The Supreme Court's adopted disposition was to allow Muttoo's appeal and hold that a landlord who retired before receiving the Government's notice to vacate could nevertheless receive section 14A benefits. Its reasoning rejected the High Court's serving-Government-employee restriction, treated the pending earlier eviction petition as founded on different statutory grounds, held that the mixed residential and professional letting of F-9 did not defeat section 14A, and applied the restricted section 25B leave-to-contest framework. It also rejected the attempt to import the separate section 14(1)(e) requirements through section 25C, while recognizing that an applicable order for recovery remains subject to the two-month possession period. The judgment's operative holding must be distinguished from an independent all-premises-satisfied computation and from actual physical delivery of possession.
records.stage: Supreme Court final appellate disposition

records.text: The judgment records Muttoo's ownership and letting of F-9 and his Government allotment at C-II/77, but it does not conduct a separate title-registration trial, identify an independently verified registration instrument, or establish a precise post-retirement date on which Muttoo physically occupied the Government accommodation. The finding that retirement did not independently bar section 14A benefits should not be converted into a finding that every potential occupation-related factual question was separately tried and resolved.
records.stage: Limits of section 14A factual reconstruction

records.text: The Government's general policy was dated 9 September 1975, and the individual notice was served on Muttoo on 9 December 1975. Section 14A specifies that the right accrues from the qualifying governmental order. The dates of the policy decision and service of the individual notice are recorded, but the Court does not separately determine that every legally relevant order-date question is resolved by treating one of those dates as the unique accrual date for an independent rule computation. Nor does the judgment establish that Muttoo actually incurred or paid the conditional penal licence charges mentioned in the notice.
records.stage: Limits of qualifying-order chronology and conditional consequences

records.text: Although the Supreme Court allowed the landlord's appeal and confirmed the availability of section 14A benefits notwithstanding prior retirement, the supplied judgment does not establish a date on which Muttoo recovered actual physical possession of F-9 or a date on which Nandi surrendered it. The Rent Controller's 10 March 1976 eviction order had been set aside by the High Court before the Supreme Court's appellate decision. The Supreme Court also expressly recognized the statutory two-month period measured from an applicable recovery order. It would therefore be unsupported to infer that possession was physically transferred on the date of the original Rent Controller order, on the date of the Supreme Court judgment, or automatically upon expiration of a calculated period.
records.stage: Final disposition and limits of execution-stage evidence

records.text: The separate conditional-rule representation of section 14A, identified as R1, remains in state UNKNOWN rather than TRUE. Its recorded premise states are UNKNOWN for residential ownership, UNKNOWN for qualifying occupation of Government-allotted accommodation, UNKNOWN for the qualifying order, and TRUE for the landlord-tenant letting connection. The Supreme Court's decision that Muttoo was entitled to section 14A benefits is an attributed judicial holding and must not silently override those independent premise states. The supplied judgment supports reconstruction of what the Court decided, but the conditional model does not independently establish all R1 inputs as verified TRUE.
records.stage: Independent rule-computation limitation and Supreme Court disposition

records.text: The Supreme Court did not finally adjudicate the misuse, subletting, or bona fide residential-need allegations underlying the earlier 1974 eviction case. Its discussion of section 14(1)(e) and earlier mixed-use authorities was undertaken to distinguish that ground from section 14A, not to establish that Muttoo proved every element of section 14(1)(e). The Court also did not determine that professional activity was actually conducted at F-9 merely because the lease authorized residential and professional use. No final result of the earlier proceeding can be inferred from the disposition of the section 14A appeal.
records.stage: Limits of earlier proceeding and mixed-use comparison
